hints: Focus on what alkaline hydrolysis does, it splits the ester at the COO link to give a carboxylate part and an alcohol part.
Work out the two halves of ethyl butanoate, the butanoate part comes from a 4-carbon acid and the ethyl part comes from a 2-carbon alcohol.
Remember that with excess NaOH the acid half is neutralised to its sodium salt, while the alcohol half stays as a neutral alcohol.
walkthrough:
**Split the ester name into its two halves**

Think of an ester as acid part + alcohol part joined together. Ethyl butanoate means ethyl alcohol joined to butanoic acid.

Structure to picture:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$

**Apply the alkaline hydrolysis rule**

With dilute $\text{NaOH}$, the ester bond breaks and $\text{OH}^-$ joins the acid side. That acid is then neutralised to a sodium carboxylate salt, while the alkyl group forms the free alcohol.

General pattern:
$$\text{RCO}_2\text{R'} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{RCO}_2\text{Na} + \text{R'OH}$$

**Put in the real groups and conclude**

Here $\text{R} = \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{R'} = \text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, so the products are sodium butanoate plus ethanol.

Full equation:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Na} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$
That sodium salt matches one of the listed options.

options.A: Correct. The butanoate part ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2$) combines with $\text{Na}^+$ from NaOH to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$, sodium butanoate. This is exactly what alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) produces alongside ethanol.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$ is sodium ethanoate, which would come from an ethyl ethanoate ester. You have mixed up butanoate (4 carbons) with ethanoate (2 carbons). Always count the carbons in the acid part.
options.C: Incorrect. The alcohol product is neutral ethanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, not sodium ethoxide, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{ONa}$. Alkoxides form from reactive metals like Na, not from dilute aqueous NaOH hydrolysis.
options.D: Incorrect. Water is a reactant in acid hydrolysis and is consumed, not a product here. In alkaline hydrolysis with NaOH, the products are the carboxylate salt and the alcohol, with no water formed.
